chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated from al-Ash'ari, from Samakah ibn Mihran, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Verily, Allah, the Exalted, did not send any Prophet or Imam except that he is more knowledgeable than what is to come.'
He said: 'If that is so, then verily Allah, the Exalted, did not grant people knowledge of what is to come except through the Prophet or the Imam.'
So if you wish to know, look at what events occur; if they match what the Prophet or the Imam said, then they are from Allah, and if they contradict, then they are from Satan.
He said: 'And this is a sound hadith in our view.'

key_terms.إِمَام: Imam (leader, specifically the infallible successors in Shia theology)
key_terms.النَّبِيُّ: The Prophet (Muhammad, peace be upon him)
key_terms.الْأُمُور: Events/Affairs (future occurrences or matters of state)
key_terms.صَحِيح: Sound/Correct (a technical term in hadith sciences indicating reliability)

ai.seo_question: How do Shia Muslims verify the authenticity of future events based on the teachings of the Prophet and Imams?
ai.summary: In *Kamal al-Din*, Shaykh al-Saduq utilizes this hadith to anchor the doctrine of *Ismah* (infallibility) and *Ilm al-Ghayb* (knowledge of the unseen) as essential criteria for validating the Imamate against rival sects. It emphasizes that while prophets possess comprehensive knowledge granted by Allah, the Imams inherit this specific divine attribute, thereby distinguishing their authoritative guidance from the partial or deceptive claims of others. This establishes a theological boundary where true prophetic continuity is measured by the exclusive bestowal of unseen knowledge upon the divinely appointed leaders.
